Notes: Emek Shaveh (archaeological NGO) summary of the Tel Rumeida (Tel Hebron) excavations: 'The settlement was destroyed and abandoned in 586 BCE', followed by a gap until the site was 'revived again in the Hellenist and early Roman periods (350 BCE - 1st century CE)'. Documented abandonment of the ancient mound at the Babylonian conquest; note that Nehemiah 11:25 (separate row) has Judahites living in Kiriath-arba (Hebron) in the Persian period, so the absence may apply to the tel only. Year Established -700 (c.): earliest documented Judahite presence = royal Judahite 'lmlk Hebron' stamped jar handles of Hezekiah's reign (c. 700 BCE), 13 of which were found at Hebron itself (per the LMLK seal literature); earlier biblical traditions (Abraham, Caleb, David) are not counted as documented presence.

Nehemiah 11:25: 'some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba [= Hebron] and its villages' (list of Judahite settlements in the time of Nehemiah, c. 445-433 BCE; date c., Persian period). Literary attestation of Judahite residents after the return; no size given. Historicity of the list for the Hebron area (which lay outside the province of Yehud, in the Edomite/Idumean zone) is debated.

Emek Shaveh guide timeline: in the Hellenistic period (332-167 BCE; midpoint used, c.) 'Edomites settle in the area of Mount Hebron'; the guide states that 'the remains from the Hellenistic period do not provide evidence of a Jewish presence in Hebron'. Event: Hebron becomes an Idumean (Edomite) town. Population blank: absence of evidence, not a positively documented absence.

1 Maccabees 5:65: Judas Maccabeus and his brothers 'fought the descendants of Esau [Idumeans] in the land to the south', struck Hebron and its villages, tore down its strongholds and burned its towers (c. 164/163 BCE; date c.). Parallel: Josephus, Antiquities 12.8.6 (12.353). Event: Judean raid on Idumean-held Hebron; no Jewish resident population indicated.

Emek Shaveh guide timeline: 'Yohanan Horkanus I conquers Edom, including Hebron' (dated 125 BCE in this source; other works date Hyrcanus' conquest of Idumea c. 112 BCE). Event: incorporation of Hebron into the Hasmonean state and Judaization (conversion) of the Idumean inhabitants; thereafter the population is Jewish (largely of Idumean origin).

Farhi and Ben-Shlomo, Tel Aviv 43 (2016), abstract: new numismatic evidence from Tel Hebron (Tell Rumeida) 'indicates that a Second Temple period settlement was located on the biblical mound'; the excavation revealed 'a Hasmonean through Late Roman-Early Byzantine domestic and industrial quarter', shedding light on the 'ethnic structure of the town of Hebron in particular during the Hasmonean and Early Roman periods'. Year = Hasmonean period midpoint (140-37 BCE). Presence of a settlement; full text (coin list) not accessed.

Ben-Shlomo (BAR / Bible History Daily): 2014 excavations by David Ben-Shlomo and Emanuel Eisenberg at Tel Hebron revealed four occupational phases 'from the time of the late Hasmoneans (c. 100-37 B.C.E.) to the Bar-Kokhba Revolt'; residential houses, pottery workshops, wine and oil presses, and 'two large stepped pools, which we were able to identify as mikva'ot', 'common in nearly all Second Temple period Jewish settlements in Judea'. Year = midpoint of late Hasmonean phase (c.). Archaeological evidence of a Jewish town (domestic and industrial quarter); no population estimate given.

Emek Shaveh guide (dissenting view): a stepped street 'originally built in the 1st century BCE' ends at a reservoir 'interpreted as a ritual bath'; plastered reservoirs dated 'between the Hasmonean period (the 2nd century BCE) and the late Roman period'; the guide questions the miqveh identification and notes 'the use of ritual baths was also common among the Edomites'. Also an early Roman pottery workshop, two wine presses and an olive press. Year 1st c. BCE midpoint (c.). Settlement presence; Jewish identity of the evidence contested by this source.

Jewish Virtual Library: 'King Herod (reigned 37-4 BCE) built the base of the present structure - the 12-meter-high wall - over the Tomb of the Patriarchs' (Machpelah enclosure); the page also states the city had earlier been incorporated into the Hasmonean kingdom by John Hyrcanus. Year = Herodian midpoint (c.). Event: monumental Jewish royal construction at Hebron (attribution to Herod is mainstream but not stated by Josephus).

Walla news report (23 July 2017) on Ariel University / IAA excavations at Tel Hebron led by Prof. David Ben-Shlomo: two large public miqvaot and chalk (limestone) stone vessels 'found in the Hasmonean and Early Roman layers' of the tel; the excavators conclude 'there was a Jewish population in Hebron throughout the Second Temple period'. Year = early Roman midpoint (63 BCE-70 CE; c.). Archaeological evidence of Jewish residents; no count.

Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.7 (4.529-533): Simon bar Giora marched into Idumea and took 'the city Hebron' without bloodshed, plundering much grain and fruit; Josephus describes it as a 'small city' where monuments of Abraham's descendants 'of very fine marble' were shown. Date c. 68/69 CE (before Simon entered Jerusalem in Xanthicus/Nisan of the third year of the war, 69 CE). Literary attestation of an inhabited (Judaized Idumean) small town; no figures (Simon's 40,000 followers are an army, not residents).

Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.9 (4.554): Cerealis, Vespasian's officer, 'went to Hebron, another very ancient city', broke into it by force, slew 'what multitude and young men were left therein' and 'burnt down the city' (summer 69 CE, after Vespasian left Caesarea on 5 Daesius). Event: destruction of Hebron in the Great Revolt; casualties not counted; Population blank because the source does not state that no Jews remained.

Walla report (2017) on the Tel Hebron excavations: a house with a cellar used as a kitchen or pantry that 'was burned in the days of the Great Revolt', with coins of the Great Revolt (plus one Bar Kokhba coin from a later phase). Archaeological evidence of Jewish domestic occupation destroyed c. 68-69 CE (date c.), consistent with Josephus' account of the burning of Hebron.
